name: Beth Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government, and what you say here is confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Beth Alvarez, 58, and I got my vocational certificate after caring for my father for years. I’m the junior lineworker on a crew that builds and repairs power lines for the electricity company. At seven I’m usually checking the truck inventory, then setting barriers while the lead worker tests a line. I enjoy the moment a whole street gets power back, but I still need someone to check my knots and the climb takes longer than it takes Rosa.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do work and home fit together now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Luis runs the counter at a hardware shop, and our son and daughter are grown and live elsewhere. We’ve saved about four months of bills, which took a long time on ordinary wages. I use an AI app sometimes to turn training notes into questions, but I only trust answers after I check the manual. I’m a union member because the crew needs a voice on safety, though I want to see a new tool actually work before I argue for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that a quicker paperwork system would be welcome, provided nobody calls it a reason to rush a repair. The pole and the switch still need us to check them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our shifts would probably carry on, yet my junior place is never certain if the company trims a crew. Four months saved gives us a pause, not a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my rostered line shifts and the Thursday practice climb with Rosa, our lead lineworker. Starting now I’d ask payroll for a written account of my retirement contributions; in 2029 I’d keep checking each monthly statement against my own notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly level about AI fading. I still have the familiar worry that one bad knee could change our budget faster than any software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does being junior show up on a repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter I needed Rosa to redo a splice I had dressed badly. I would rather be corrected in daylight than have a fault appear in someone’s kitchen later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your household do if pay dipped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Luis lost a shop shift, we would pause the small trips we make to see our daughter. The savings are there for a hard spell, not for an early farewell to work.

say: I’d welcome **faster paperwork** if line crews still get enough time for safety checks.
I’d remind coworkers that **poles and switches** still require careful human inspection.
think: I think my **line shifts** are likely to continue, though a junior place can be cut.
Our **four-month cushion** buys time but cannot fund retirement.
do: Keep taking **rostered shifts** and Thursday practice climbs with Rosa.
Request a **retirement contribution statement** and check it against my notebook.
feel: I feel **fairly level**, with a separate worry about my knees and household pay.
S0.quote: Four months saved gives us a pause, not a retirement plan.
fieldNote: Beth treats safety as a practiced skill, recalling a **bad splice** corrected before it caused a fault.
Her moderate cushion softens the immediate fear, while **physical strain** and junior standing keep her from feeling secure.

steps.text: Take rostered repairs and Thursday practice climbs with Rosa
Request written retirement contributions and compare monthly statements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my union branch to examine the new job schedules, because a screen misses the wood above us. An algorithm will not see a rotten crossarm from the office. I would accept a route app after another crew has tried it and reported the misses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suspect dispatch and purchasing will shrink first, then the repair crew may be asked to cover more calls per day. Luis’s counter work could lose some customer questions to AI too, so our four months might be tested from both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the safety representative to compare three months of actual repair times with any new schedule. In 2029 I’d keep working the line, try the proven route app on a supervised shift, and start setting aside twenty extra per pay if our hours hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful rather than helpless. A tool that saves a wasted drive would be nice; a target that steals testing time would make me angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What repair would a schedule miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Cedar Road last month we found a cracked insulator after the office estimate said half an hour. I wrote the real finish time down because that is the sort of evidence the branch needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide what to cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Luis the hours on both our payslips before we change spending. We can cut restaurant meals, but I do not want to pretend a smaller grocery bill solves two lost jobs.

say: I’d ask our **union branch** to inspect new schedules against real repair times.
I’d try a **route app** after another crew has shown where it fails.
think: I expect **dispatch and purchasing** to shrink before hands-on repair shifts.
Luis’s **shop counter** could also lose customer questions, testing both incomes.
do: Compare **repair times** with new job schedules.
Keep taking **line shifts** and trial a proven route app under supervision.
Set aside **twenty extra per pay** if both work schedules hold.
feel: I feel **watchful** about efficiency and angry at any pressure to rush tests.
S1.quote: An algorithm will not see a rotten crossarm from the office.
fieldNote: Beth will test software only after **peer evidence**, a clear expression of her measured openness to change.
She sees a two-income risk because **Luis’s shop** may lose routine customer questions as dispatch changes.

steps.text: Bring three months of repair times to the union safety representative
Keep taking paid line shifts in 2029
Trial a proven AI route app on a supervised shift
Set aside twenty extra per pay while both schedules hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full thinking AI in 2028 could reshape our office while we still repair lines by hand. I would ask management and the union to put actual dates and placement rules in writing before capable robots reach linework around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 when the office changes and only 63 when a robot might take a climb. I do not think being careful makes my junior job safe once a machine can do the physical repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask the training officer whether the utility will fund a cable-testing certificate, and I’d enroll if there is a paid place. In 2029 I’d keep line shifts while they exist, put our restaurant money aside, and apply to the other utility’s trainee testing post if a vacancy opens; I’d ask the union about placement before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened, mainly because those are short years at our age. I can picture myself making breakfast and quietly counting how many paydays are left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis and I would keep our four-month reserve for rent and medicine, and stop the Friday meals out. I would tell our grown children the truth about the uncertainty, without asking them to become our safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a testing certificate protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Testing could also be done by a robot later, so I would not call the certificate a shield. It would let me compete for a paid place while the transition is still happening.

say: I’d ask for **written placement rules** before hands-on robots reach linework around 2031.
I’d distinguish **2028 office change** from the later threat to physical repair.
think: At **63**, I could lose junior line shifts before retirement is affordable.
My care with repairs does not make me **robot proof** once machines can climb.
do: Request a **funded cable-testing place** and enroll if one exists.
Keep **line shifts** in 2029 and apply to a trainee testing vacancy if offered.
Stop **Friday restaurant meals** and ask the union about placement.
feel: I feel **frightened** by a short runway and uncertain paydays.
S2.quote: I do not think being careful makes my junior job safe once a machine can do the physical repair.
fieldNote: Beth’s proposed certificate is conditional on a **funded place**, and she recognizes testing may also be automated later.
She would preserve the **four-month reserve** for necessities and stop Friday meals rather than rely on grown children.

steps.text: Enroll in a funded cable-testing certificate if a paid place exists
Keep taking paid line shifts through 2029
Apply to the other utility’s trainee testing post if vacant
Stop Friday restaurant meals and protect rent money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our branch that five years is enough to negotiate a fair route for older junior workers if we start now. Thinking AI would reach scheduling and records by 2031, while robots could reach line repairs around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 at the first date and 66 at the second. I hope to slow down by then, but I cannot promise Luis we can retire without seeing actual contribution figures and our future bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d get the contribution statement, keep my certificate current, and ask the union to seek paid places in testing and maintenance. In 2032 I’d take a line shift if offered and apply for an internal inspection vacancy; before 2034 Luis and I would work out whether we could reduce hours or still need full wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wary but able to put dates on the calendar. There is enough time to make requests, and also enough time for a company to delay answering them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would inspection be a lasting role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The internal inspection post is only a bridge if people still do inspections then. I have seen a camera find a fault, and I know a capable robot might later do that whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my daughter the real pension statement once I have it, because she keeps saying I should rest more. I do not want my daughter to think my body alone can decide when I stop earning.

say: I’d urge the **union branch** to negotiate paid routes before 2031.
I’d tell coworkers **2034 robots** could change physical repair after office work changes.
think: I may still need **full wages at 66**, despite hoping to slow down.
An inspection vacancy could be a **temporary bridge**, not a permanent refuge.
do: Get my **contribution statement** and keep the line certificate current.
Apply for an **internal inspection vacancy** during 2032 if one exists.
Ask the union to seek **paid places** before 2034.
feel: I feel **wary but organized**, with calendar time to press for answers.
S3.quote: I do not want my daughter to think my body alone can decide when I stop earning.
fieldNote: Beth wants to match retirement wishes to **actual contribution figures**, not her daughter’s understandable wish that she rest.
She calls inspection a bridge because **camera technology** already handles parts of the task and robots may follow.

steps.text: Get a contribution statement before deciding whether to reduce hours
Keep the line certificate current and take offered line shifts
Apply for an internal inspection vacancy in 2032 if available
Ask the union to negotiate paid testing and maintenance places

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell friends a decade lets the crew plan, but workers should see the plan before they are too old to use it. Thinking AI may take the records in 2036; capable robots could do the repairs around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when the thinking work changes and 71 when robots climb. I might be retired by then, yet four months saved now is no proof, especially if Luis’s shop hours fall earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask for a clear pension estimate and keep taking the safe line jobs I can do. In 2037 I’d take paid mentoring shifts if the company offered them, and Luis and I would compare pension income with rent before deciding whether to retire; if the gap stayed large, I’d apply for a lighter warehouse role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more hopeful with a decade than with two years. I also feel stubborn about making the numbers visible before anyone calls us secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you teach a newer worker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could teach a new worker how to set barriers and check a truck, though I am not the person to teach difficult splices yet. A mentoring offer would have to be paid work, not a polite send-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you live with your children if money tightened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not move in with either grown child just to fill a gap in a pension guess. Luis and I would first check the statement, our bills and what other paid work is really open.

say: I’d ask for a **visible workforce plan** while older workers can still use it.
I’d explain **2036 records** and around 2039 hands-on robots are different stages.
think: I could be retired by **71**, but present savings do not prove it.
Luis’s **shop hours** could shrink earlier, changing our retirement figures.
do: Request a **pension estimate** and continue safe paid line jobs.
Take **paid mentoring shifts** in 2037 if the company offers them.
Apply for a **lighter warehouse role** if retirement income falls short.
feel: I feel **more hopeful**, while insisting on real numbers before feeling secure.
S4.quote: A mentoring offer would have to be paid work, not a polite send-off.
fieldNote: Beth sees a specific possible mentoring task, **truck and barrier checks**, while admitting complex splices remain beyond her teaching skill.
She keeps future **warehouse work** conditional on an actual retirement shortfall and avoids assuming support from grown children.

steps.text: Request a pension estimate and compare it with rent
Take safe line jobs and paid mentoring shifts if offered in 2037
Apply for a lighter warehouse role if pension income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the line robots could arrive while I am 63 and still need a wage. A funded training place tied to a real vacancy would help, along with an agreement about notice and placement. Luis and I can budget around facts, but we cannot budget around a reassuring speech.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask why I came to linework so late. Caring for my father was work too, even when nobody paid me. I am proud I got the certificate and started again, though I still need Rosa to check the hard parts.

headlineQuote: Caring for my father was work too, even when nobody paid me.
portrait: Beth is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who earned a vocational certificate after years of caring for her father.
She and partner Luis have about **four months of bills** saved, while both incomes could change before retirement.
She tests new technology after **other crews** prove it and checks AI study answers against the manual.
Across scenarios, she seeks **union backed placement** and funded training, but checks actual pension figures before planning retirement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Beth most because capable line robots could arrive when she still needs a wage.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded training place** linked to a vacancy, plus notice and placement rules, would let her household budget.
